This necessitates ongoing research into methods that can minimize the memory footprint and enhance the performance of n-gram models without sacrificing accuracy. While techniques like pruning and smoothing have proven effective in mitigating some of the issues, they often address the problem at a statistical level rather than a structural one. The underlying data structures remain a bottleneck. Consequently, there’s a continuing need for innovative approaches to the representation and indexing of n-gram models that directly address the memory and speed challenges. Recent advancements in succinct data structures offer a promising avenue for exploration. Specifically, double-array structures—compact, space-efficient data structures traditionally used for representing compressed sequences—have demonstrated considerable potential in various applications. In this paper, we investigate and propose a novel methodology for constructing efficient n-gram language models based on the principles of double-array structures. Our approach centers around representing a backwards suffix tree, a fundamental data structure underlying n-gram models, directly within a double-array framework. This allows for a significantly more compact representation compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we introduce two key optimization techniques to further enhance the efficiency of our implementation. Firstly, we explore the possibility of embedding probabilities directly into the often-unused spaces within the double-array, effectively reducing the overall model size without impacting functionality. Secondly, we propose a strategic re-mapping of word IDs within the model, designed to cluster frequently occurring words together, thereby minimizing search distances and accelerating query processing. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of building exceptionally large language models by leveraging a division technique that allows the model to be distributed across multiple double-array structures. We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating substantial improvements in both model size and query speed, particularly when both optimization techniques are combined. Our results suggest that double-array structures offer a viable and compelling alternative for constructing efficient and scalable n-gram language models, paving the way for more resource-friendly NLP applications.

The study of semantic change – how the meanings of words evolve over time – has long been a core area of interest for linguists and computational social scientists. Understanding these shifts is crucial for historical linguistics, digital humanities research, and even for improving the robustness of natural language processing systems that grapple with language's dynamic nature. Traditional approaches to modeling semantic change have largely relied on analyzing diachronic distributional data – observing how words co-occur with other words across different time periods. Early computational methods often treated time as a discrete variable, partitioning the historical record into distinct intervals and comparing word vectors between these periods. While these methods have yielded valuable insights, they frequently struggle to capture the nuanced, continuous nature of semantic drift—the subtle and gradual shifts in meaning that characterize linguistic evolution. Moreover, evaluating the effectiveness of these models has been challenging, often relying on qualitative assessment or indirect proxies for semantic similarity. Recent advancements in deep learning have revolutionized numerous areas of NLP, offering powerful tools for modeling complex relationships within data. However, their application to the specific challenge of diachronic distributional semantics remains relatively unexplored. Previous neural models have primarily focused on capturing semantic similarity *within* a single time period, or on identifying synchronic relationships between words. Addressing the temporal dimension—tracking how those relationships evolve—requires fundamentally different modeling strategies. This paper introduces a novel deep neural network model designed specifically to capture and quantify semantic shift over time. Recognizing that semantic change is rarely abrupt but rather a continuous process, we eschew the discrete time-slice approach of previous work. Instead, our model represents time as a continuous variable, allowing us to model a word’s usage as a continuous function of time. This allows for the capture of gradual semantic shifts and provides a more detailed picture of how word meanings evolve. Critically, we believe that the ability to model time as a continuous variable is paramount to capturing the real-world nuances of semantic change. To facilitate rigorous evaluation of our model, we have developed a new synthetic task—a ‘semantic trajectory prediction’ task—designed to quantitatively assess how accurately a model captures a word’s semantic evolution. This task moves beyond simple comparison of word vectors at different time points and instead requires the model to predict the semantic ‘path’ a word takes over time. We use this task to demonstrate the superiority of our continuous-time approach compared to traditional discrete-time modeling strategies. Finally, we investigate the utility of the model's derivatives – the rate of change of a word’s semantic representation over time – as a measure of the speed of lexical change. We posit that the steepness of a word's semantic trajectory can provide a quantifiable measure of how rapidly a word’s meaning is evolving, offering a valuable tool for linguistic historians and potentially shedding light on the social and cultural factors driving semantic change. Through experimentation and analysis, we demonstrate the potential of using such derivatives as a robust proxy for measuring the rate of lexical evolution. Our work represents a significant step toward a more sophisticated and quantitatively rigorous understanding of how language changes over time.

Machine translation has long been a central challenge in natural language processing, driving significant advancements across various modeling paradigms. Early successes were largely attributed to phrase-based statistical machine translation (PBSMT) systems, which decomposed sentences into non-overlapping phrases and modeled translation probabilities based on phrase alignment. However, PBSMT suffers from a fundamental limitation: the phrasal independence assumption. This assumption dictates that the probability of translating a sequence of phrases can be calculated as the product of probabilities of translating each individual phrase, neglecting crucial dependencies between them. This simplification, while computationally efficient, often leads to suboptimal translations, particularly when handling long-range dependencies or context-sensitive language. Recent years have seen a surge in the application of neural machine translation (NMT), particularly sequence-to-sequence models utilizing recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants, offering the potential to overcome this phrasal independence bottleneck. While NMT models demonstrate impressive translation quality, they often struggle to effectively utilize contextual information beyond a relatively narrow window due to limitations inherent in the recurrent nature of RNNs and the vanishing gradient problem, especially when grappling with extended input sequences. This motivates the exploration of hybrid approaches that combine aspects of PBSMT and NMT to leverage the strengths of both. In this paper, we introduce a novel recurrent neural network-based tuple sequence model (RNNTSM) designed specifically to address the shortcomings of PBSMT by moving beyond the restrictive phrasal independence assumption. Our RNNTSM aims to capture more comprehensive and arbitrary long-range contextual information during the estimation of translation probabilities for tuples—contiguous sequences of words—within the source and target languages. By embedding these tuples into a continuous vector space and employing an RNN to model the sequence of these embeddings, we seek to represent the interdependencies between tuples and generate more fluent and accurate translations. However, the implementation of RNNTSM is complicated by a significant data sparsity issue. The inherent complexity of natural language results in an incredibly large tuple vocabulary, far exceeding the size of typical bilingual training datasets. This leads to insufficient training data for many individual tuples, hampering the model's ability to learn meaningful representations and estimate reliable probabilities. To mitigate this critical problem, we propose two key innovations. First, we introduce a factorized RNNTSM, which decomposes the bilingual tuple representation into separate source and target-side representations, allowing for more efficient learning. Second, we explore decomposing phrasal tuples into smaller word-level tuples, thereby augmenting the training data with a finer-grained representation of the language and providing a richer set of features for capturing subtle relationships. Through extensive experimentation on the IWSLT2012 test sets 1, we demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly improves translation quality compared to state-of-the-art PBSMT systems and RNN language models, delivering notable BLEU score improvements on both English-French and English-German translation tasks. We believe that our RNNTSM and its enhancements represent a valuable step toward bridging the gap between traditional phrase-based models and modern neural approaches, offering a potentially powerful framework for future machine translation research.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) plays a pivotal role in shaping the US macroeconomic landscape, wielding significant influence over financial markets and economic activity through its monetary policy decisions. While the FOMC’s actions – primarily adjustments to the federal funds rate target – have long been scrutinized, the *communication* surrounding these actions has gained increasing attention as a potentially powerful and distinct driver of market expectations and, subsequently, interest rates. Forward guidance, a relatively recent tool in the central banker’s toolkit, highlights the importance of clarifying the likely future path of monetary policy to influence market behavior. However, the efficacy of forward guidance, and indeed the information content embedded within all FOMC communications, remains a subject of ongoing debate and empirical investigation. This paper delves into the intricate relationship between the textual content of FOMC statements and the subsequent movements of US Treasury rates, aiming to quantify the predictive power of these communications on both short- and medium-term interest rate behavior. Existing research examining the impact of FOMC communication has often focused on broad market reactions or aggregate measures of uncertainty. While these studies provide valuable insights, they tend to overlook the nuanced ways in which specific phrases, topics, and sentiments within FOMC statements can affect different segments of the yield curve. For instance, discussions surrounding inflation expectations might disproportionately impact longer-term Treasury yields, while comments on the labor market could exert a stronger influence on short-term rates. Recognizing this heterogeneity, our study moves beyond simplistic measures of communication impact to adopt a more granular, content-driven approach. We hypothesize that specific linguistic patterns and recurring themes within FOMC statements, when processed and analyzed, can effectively predict directional movements in Treasury rates. To operationalize this hypothesis, we leverage advanced text mining and machine learning techniques. Critically, we acknowledge that the language relevant to predicting short-term interest rate movements may differ significantly from that relevant to longer-term rates. Consequently, we employ a supervised learning framework that allows the model to learn distinct topic representations optimized for accurately predicting the direction of each dependent variable—the Target Federal Funds Rate, the Effective Federal Funds Rate, and longer-term Treasury rates. This targeted approach allows for a more sophisticated understanding of how different aspects of FOMC communication exert their influence on various points along the yield curve. Our methodology involves constructing a comprehensive dataset encompassing FOMC statements from 1999 to 2016, alongside corresponding daily Treasury rates. We then utilize topic modeling and feature engineering to extract relevant textual features from the FOMC statements. These features are subsequently fed into predictive models, trained to forecast the direction of interest rate movements. We evaluate our models' performance across multiple training-test splits to ensure robustness and generalizability. Furthermore, we conduct a comparative analysis, examining predictive accuracy both with and without controlling for established macroeconomic and market factors known to influence interest rates. This allows us to isolate the incremental contribution of FOMC communication content to our predictions. In the following sections, we detail our data and methodology, present our empirical results, and discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the communication strategies of the Federal Reserve and their impact on financial markets.

The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has long recognized the power of distributional semantics – the idea that a word’s meaning is reflected in the company it keeps. Vector space models, such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText, have revolutionized our ability to represent words as continuous vectors, capturing nuanced semantic relationships like synonymy and analogy. However, a persistent challenge with these representations is their tendency to conflate opposing meanings. While synonyms cluster closely together in these vector spaces, so too do antonyms – a phenomenon that undermines the accuracy and interpretability of subsequent NLP applications. This proximity of opposites can be particularly detrimental in tasks requiring precise semantic understanding, such as sentiment analysis, question answering, and semantic search. Traditional spectral clustering methods, frequently employed to group words based on their vector representations, are inherently susceptible to this issue. Spectral clustering approaches construct a graph where nodes represent words, and edge weights reflect the similarity between them, typically derived from the cosine similarity of their corresponding vectors. This naturally leads to clustering where words with high similarity—including antonyms—are grouped together. While such approaches excel at identifying synonyms, they fail to explicitly account for the crucial distinction between positive and negative semantic associations. The lack of explicit negation representation embeds a fundamental limitation in the resulting clusters: they lack the ability to distinguish between opposing concepts. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach termed "Signed Spectral Clustering." This method elegantly combines the strengths of distributionally derived word embeddings and explicit lexical knowledge, specifically incorporating information from established thesauri. Our core innovation lies in augmenting the similarity graph with negative edge weights derived from antonym relationships present in these thesauri. By purposefully representing antonymy with negative connections, we force the spectral clustering algorithm to differentiate between converging and diverging semantic relationships. This allows for the creation of clusters that simultaneously capture distributional similarities (synonymy) and opposing meanings (antonymy), resulting in a richer and more semantically coherent representation of word relationships. The effectiveness of our approach hinges on a computationally efficient implementation. We leverage randomized spectral decomposition (Halko et al., 2011) to achieve scalability, enabling the processing of large vocabularies. Furthermore, we utilize sparse matrix representations to optimize memory usage and computational speed, crucial for practical application. This combination of semantic enrichment and algorithmic efficiency positions Signed Spectral Clustering as a valuable tool for various NLP tasks. In this paper, we detail the mathematical formulation of our algorithm, demonstrate its scalability, and present comprehensive evaluations using both human-annotated word similarity datasets and a sentiment prediction benchmark. Our results demonstrate that Signed Spectral Clustering significantly improves cluster quality and enhances performance in downstream tasks compared to traditional spectral clustering methods relying solely on distributional semantics. The burgeoning field of natural language processing has seen remarkable progress in tasks ranging from machine translation to question answering. However, a crucial gap remains in bridging the semantic chasm between human-level instruction and actionable robotic control. Humans routinely communicate goals – “make me a cup of coffee,” “tidy up the living room,” “find the blue book” – without explicitly detailing the sequence of steps required to achieve them. This ability to infer and execute actions based on high-level, often underspecified, intentions is a hallmark of human intelligence, and replicating it in artificial systems remains a significant challenge. Current approaches to robotic task execution often rely on explicitly programmed sequences or meticulously curated datasets mapping instructions to actions, a methodology that struggles to generalize to novel situations or adapt to variations in environment and task complexity. Statistical methods, while successful in certain limited domains, fundamentally lack the capacity to reason about the underlying dynamics of the environment necessary for interpreting instructions that require significant inference. This paper tackles the problem of translating high-level instructions into sequences of commands within an external environment – a capacity we term *instructional interpretation*. Our core argument is that successful interpretation necessitates an understanding, albeit potentially incomplete, of the environmental dynamics; i.e., how actions transform states and ultimately contribute to achieving the intended goal. We propose a novel approach that learns an environment model *concurrently* with a policy for translating instructions into actions. This environment model is not hand-engineered or pre-defined, but rather automatically derived through interaction and observation, encoding the relationships between states, transitions, and the commands that trigger those transitions. The key innovation lies in our efficient approximate method for learning this environment model, framed within a policy gradient reinforcement learning framework. Previous work has explored environment model learning for robotics, but often under the assumption of a fixed, known policy or utilizing computationally expensive methods that limit scalability. Our design prioritizes efficiency, enabling rapid learning for complex, high-level instruction mapping tasks that are beyond the reach of conventional statistical techniques. By integrating the environment model learning directly into the policy learning process, we create a synergistic loop where the policy benefits from a richer understanding of the environment, and the environment model is refined by the need to support increasingly sophisticated action sequences. Furthermore, our approach moves beyond the limitations of purely data-driven methods. While large datasets of instruction-action pairs can be useful, they are inherently limited in their coverage of possible scenarios. Our learned environment model allows the system to generalize to instructions or situations not explicitly encountered during training, enabling a degree of compositional reasoning and adaptation that is vital for robust and general-purpose robotic assistance. This paper presents a system capable of interpreting high-level instructions and leveraging a learned environment model to guide action selection, paving the way for more flexible and intelligent robotic agents. We will detail the architecture, training procedure, experimental results, and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a challenging simulated environment. In the following sections, we will elaborate on the design of our system, including the environment model representation, the learning algorithm, and the experimental setup.

Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) has emerged as a powerful and increasingly popular framework for semantic representation, offering a structured, graph-based depiction of sentence meaning that transcends syntactic structure and captures core semantic relations. Unlike traditional semantic representations tied to surface form, AMR focuses on the underlying conceptual structure, facilitating more robust and human-interpretable understanding of language. This capability makes it invaluable for tasks ranging from machine translation and question answering to dialogue systems and natural language inference. However, AMR parsing – the process of automatically converting a sentence into its corresponding AMR graph – remains a challenging endeavor, demanding systems capable of grappling with complex syntactic and semantic mappings. While significant progress has been made in recent years, achieving high accuracy and efficiency in AMR parsing continues to be a central research focus. Existing approaches to AMR parsing predominantly fall into two categories: graph-to-graph models and sequence-to-graph models. Graph-to-graph models, often based on neural networks, directly map the input sentence or a derived syntactic structure into the AMR graph. These models have demonstrated impressive performance but frequently struggle with computational complexity and data sparsity, especially when dealing with longer and more complex sentences. Sequence-to-graph models, alternatively, treat AMR parsing as a sequence labeling problem and typically utilize recurrent neural networks. While exhibiting advantages in modularity and adaptability, these too can grapple with challenges in maintaining global graph consistency and capturing long-range dependencies crucial for accurate AMR construction. In this paper, we introduce a novel transition-based algorithm for AMR parsing that leverages the strengths of both dependency parsing and graph construction techniques. Our approach adopts a two-stage framework, capitalizing on the readily available and abundant resources for dependency parsing. We first employ a pre-trained dependency parser to generate a dependency tree for the input sentence. This benefits from the vast training datasets commonly used to train dependency parsers, enabling the initial stage to achieve high syntactic accuracy. The second, and critical, stage of our system is a newly designed transition-based algorithm that systematically transforms this dependency tree into the final AMR graph. This transition-based construction is a key innovation. Existing tree-to-graph methods often suffer from high computational cost and difficulty in training due to the limited availability of annotated AMR data. By decoupling these stages, our approach alleviates these drawbacks. Furthermore, the transition actions we define are grounded in linguistic intuition and are specifically tailored to capture the recurring patterns observed in the mapping between dependency trees and AMR graphs. We argue that this linguistically driven design leads to more robust and interpretable action choices, ultimately contributing to improved parsing accuracy. Moreover, despite a theoretical worst-case complexity of O(n²), our implemented algorithm exhibits near-linear runtime performance in practice, making it scalable to sentences of significant length. Experimental results on the standard LDC AMR parsing benchmark demonstrate that our parser achieves a substantial improvement of 5% absolute in F-measure compared to the previous state-of-the-art, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach.

The relentless proliferation of news content presents a significant challenge for information consumption. Users are increasingly overwhelmed by a constant stream of headlines, making it difficult to efficiently grasp the core themes and events unfolding across diverse sources. Traditional headline generation approaches, often relying on extractive methods, merely select existing phrases from the source article, failing to provide a concise, abstractive summary of the underlying news story. While recent advancements in neural sequence-to-sequence models have shown promise in abstractive headline generation, existing methods often struggle to maintain coherence, consistency, and relevance across collections of related news articles, frequently producing generic or uninformative outputs. These shortcomings highlight the need for a more sophisticated approach that can distill the essence of a news collection into a single, informative headline. This paper introduces HEADY (Headline Abstraction through Event Pattern Clustering), a novel approach to news headline generation that leverages event pattern clustering to achieve significantly improved abstraction and coherence. Unlike purely data-driven neural approaches, HEADY incorporates linguistic knowledge gleaned from a large-scale corpus of English news articles to identify and generalize common event structures. We hypothesize that news articles, despite variations in wording, frequently describe similar underlying events. By discovering and representing these events as generalized patterns, we aim to enable headline generation that captures the overarching narrative of a news collection, rather than simply reflecting individual article content. Our core innovation lies in the utilization of a Noisy-OR model to represent these event patterns. This model allows us to capture the inherent variability in how events can be described, accommodating different syntactic structures and word choices while maintaining a consistent semantic representation. The Noisy-OR framework elegantly handles the ambiguity within natural language, recognizing that multiple surface forms can express the same event. We learn these patterns from a web-scale corpus, creating a robust and expressive knowledge base of recurring event descriptions. At inference time, HEADY operates by analyzing an unseen news collection and identifying patterns that align with the learned event structures. We query the Noisy-OR model with observed syntactic patterns from the input collection, identifying the event that best encapsulates its overall gist. Subsequently, the model retrieves the most appropriate, generalized event pattern corresponding to that event, which is then used as a template for generating an abstractive headline. This process explicitly encourages the generation of headlines that reflect the broader context of the news collection, promoting coherence and relevance. Preliminary evaluations demonstrate that HEADY significantly improves upon a state-of-the-art open-domain title abstraction method. Critically, HEADY bridges a substantial portion of the performance gap that separates abstractive methods from extractive techniques, as assessed through human evaluations of headline quality. Furthermore, HEADY achieves comparable performance to human-generated headlines when evaluated using ROUGE metrics. We believe that HEADY’s novel approach to incorporating event pattern clustering represents a significant step toward enabling more effective and informative news headline generation, facilitating better information access and comprehension in an increasingly complex media landscape. The remainder of this paper details the architecture of HEADY, describes our experimental setup, presents our evaluation results, and discusses avenues for future research.

The explosion of unstructured text data presents both a challenge and an opportunity for natural language processing. While traditional NLP techniques have largely focused on analyzing the semantic content of text – the *what* of communication – the structural organization, the *how* information is presented, remains comparatively under-explored, particularly as a means of feature engineering. Understanding the underlying structure of a document, whether a scientific paper, a legal contract, or a transcribed lecture, is often critical for downstream tasks like information extraction, summarization, and content segmentation. However, most current methods rely on content-driven approaches like TF-IDF, which, while valuable, are inherently limited in their ability to capture the crucial role of structural cues. These cues are the linguistic markers—specific words, phrases, or patterns—that signal transitions, logical connections, and the overall flow of ideas within a text. The inherent limitation of content-based methods lies in their focus on term frequency and inverse document frequency, effectively prioritizing the most statistically common words, irrespective of their function within the textual architecture. While high-frequency words like "the," "and," and content-specific keywords are undoubtedly important, they often obscure the equally, if not more, vital role played by discourse markers such as “therefore,” “however,” “in conclusion,” or even seemingly innocuous phrases whose recurring presence flags shifts in topic or argument. Consider the task of segmenting lecture transcripts: a student is more likely to perceive meaningful breaks based on cues like summarization statements and transitions, rather than solely on the prevalence of technical jargon. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a novel approach – the Rhetorical Structure Index (RSI) – designed to quantify the structural importance of words and phrases within a document. Unlike TF-IDF and related techniques, RSI is not driven by content frequency; instead, it identifies and weights elements based on their prevalence as signaling points within the document’s rhetorical architecture. Our hypothesis is that words and phrases that consistently mark shifts in topic, arguments, or narrative flow are structurally important and can provide considerably more value for tasks that rely on understanding document organization. The underlying intuition is that these elements aren't necessarily the most *frequent* keywords, but they are the most *consistent* indicators of structure. We posit that RSI offers a unique perspective on feature engineering, moving beyond simply identifying what is being discussed to assessing *how* it is being discussed. The framework leverages patterns in sequential word occurrences to identify terms whose consistent co-occurrence with specific discourse relations provides a clear structural significance. Specifically, we demonstrate that RSI-derived features outperform traditional TF-IDF features in a challenging application: segmenting unstructured lecture transcripts into meaningful segments. By focusing on rhetorical cues, we’re able to better capture the logical structure of the lecture and delineate its constituent parts, leading to more accurate and interpretable segmentation results. The remainder of this paper details the RSI methodology, presents experimental results validating its effectiveness, and discusses its potential applications and future directions within NLP.

Computational argumentation mining (AM) has emerged as a crucial area within natural language processing, aiming to automatically identify and extract argumentative structures from text. The ability to decompose text into its constituent argumentative components—claims, premises, evidence, and relations between them—holds significant potential for a diverse range of applications, from automated debate analysis and summarization to improved information retrieval and persuasive writing tools. Existing approaches to AM have largely relied on feature engineering and structured models, often incorporating hand-crafted rules and linguistic knowledge to guide the extraction process. While these methods have achieved reasonable results, they are often brittle, requiring significant domain expertise and struggling to generalize well to new datasets or argumentative styles. The recent progress in deep learning has spurred interest in leveraging neural networks to automate AM, but a truly end-to-end trainable model that can effectively capture the nuances of argumentation remains an open challenge. The core difficulty in AM lies in the inherently complex and often subtle relationships between argumentative elements. Argumentation is not merely a collection of statements; it’s a structured discourse where individual components rely on each other to form a coherent and persuasive reasoning chain. These relationships can span significant distances within a text, making it difficult for models to capture them effectively. Further complicating matters is the variability in how argumentation is expressed linguistically, with different styles, tones, and levels of explicitness across various domains and genres. Traditional approaches often struggle to account for this variability, while neural models, despite their potential for generalization, require careful design to learn and represent these argumentative dependencies. This paper explores the use of neural architectures for end-to-end computational argumentation mining, moving beyond reliance on manually engineered features. We investigate two distinct framing approaches – representing AM as a token-based dependency parsing task and as a token-based sequence tagging task – in addition to a multi-task learning setup designed to leverage related subtasks. The dependency parsing formulation aims to simultaneously identify the argumentative role of each token and the relations between them, mirroring the hierarchical structure often associated with argumentation. In contrast, the sequence tagging model focuses on assigning labels to individual tokens, classifying them into categories such as claim, premise, evidence, or non-argumentative. While dependency parsing has proven successful in a variety of NLP tasks, we hypothesized that its complexity might be unnecessary for the specific challenges of AM. Our initial experiments challenge this assumption, revealing that framing AM as a comprehensive dependency parsing problem results in surprisingly lower performance compared to simpler sequence tagging approaches. Crucially, we observe that relatively uncomplicated models based on bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks, operating as token-level sequence taggers, demonstrate robust and competitive performance across diverse AM classification scenarios. This suggests that effective long-range dependency modeling is crucial in this task, and that sophisticated structure-aware models may not necessarily be superior to more focused, local processing when properly designed. Furthermore, we explore the benefits of multi-task learning, hypothesizing that jointly training the AM model with related, ‘natural’ subtasks can improve generalization and capture complementary linguistic cues. This paper details our experimentation with these diverse approaches, analyzing their strengths and weaknesses, and ultimately offering insights into the design of effective neural architectures for end-to-end computational argumentation mining.

The pervasive challenge of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words continues to pose a significant bottleneck in the pursuit of robust and reliable large vocabulary continuous speech recognition (LVCSR) systems. While substantial advances have been made in acoustic modeling and language modeling, the inability to accurately handle words absent from the system's lexicon remains a persistent source of error, reverberating throughout the entire speech processing pipeline. These recognition failures, stemming directly from OOV words, cascade into downstream tasks such as automatic summarization, speech-to-text translation, and voice-controlled applications, ultimately degrading their performance and limiting overall usability. The downstream impact highlights the critical need for improved OOV detection mechanisms. Traditional approaches to OOV detection largely treat the problem as a binary classification task conducted on isolated segments of the recognized transcript. These methods primarily rely on localized features – acoustic probabilities, word probabilities, and sometimes simple n-gram context – to determine whether a given transcribed region represents an OOV word or a valid vocabulary item. This isolated assessment, however, neglects the powerful predictive capacity inherent in the surrounding discourse and broader context of the utterance. The very nature of language dictates that the probability of encountering a novel term is rarely independent of its neighborhood. Words are interconnected, semantically and syntactically, and the likelihood of encountering an OOV word often shifts drastically based on the preceding and subsequent words, the topic of conversation, and the speaker’s intent. Therefore, this paper proposes and investigates a novel approach to OOV detection that explicitly incorporates contextual information into the decision-making process. We argue that by jointly predicting OOV regions and leveraging a wider contextual window, we can significantly improve the accuracy and robustness of OOV detection compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Our approach moves beyond the assumption of independence between segments, instead leveraging the relational dependencies between words to inform the classification of potential OOV candidates. This contextual awareness allows the system to discern between genuine OOV words (e.g., newly coined terms, proper nouns not present in the lexicon) and potentially misrecognized in-vocabulary words that simply appear atypical within their contextual surroundings. We detail a model architecture designed to effectively capture and utilize this contextual information, demonstrating empirically on a benchmark dataset that our method leads to a remarkable reduction in missed OOV (OOV miss rate) while maintaining a competitive false alarm rate. Specifically, we achieve a significant reduction in the OOV miss rate – lowering it from 42.6% to 28.4% at a fixed 10% false alarm rate, representing a considerable step forward in the field. Our results underscore the potential of contextual modeling for improving the accuracy and reliability of OOV detection, paving the way for more robust LVCSR systems and downstream applications reliant on clean and accurate speech transcriptions. The subsequent sections elaborate on the methodological details, experimental setup, and a thorough analysis of our findings, demonstrating the efficacy of leveraging contextual information in addressing this long-standing challenge.

The burgeoning volume of data generated through social media platforms presents unprecedented opportunities to understand human behavior and preferences. While much research has focused on leveraging social media for tasks like sentiment analysis, opinion mining, and network analysis, its potential for predicting offline attributes – particularly those related to economic activity – remains relatively underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by investigating the feasibility of predicting restaurant consumption level, a tangible indicator of discretionary spending, through analysis of users’ online social media footprints. Understanding this relationship carries significant implications, offering valuable insights for both social scientists seeking to analyze patterns of consumer behavior and businesses aiming to refine targeted marketing strategies. Current approaches to consumer profiling often rely on transactional data – directly observed purchase histories. While accurate, such datasets are often proprietary, incomplete, and may not capture the multifaceted nature of consumer preferences. Social media, in contrast, offers a rich and publicly accessible source of behavioral data, reflecting users' interests, opinions, social connections, and expressed lifestyles. However, directly correlating social media activity with offline behavior is a complex challenge. The inherent noise and superficiality of some online interactions, coupled with the self-selective nature of online expression, demand sophisticated methodologies to extract meaningful signals. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel, systematic approach that combines social login data, user-generated content from Sina Weibo (a leading Chinese microblogging platform), and restaurant consumption data from Dianping (a popular Chinese review platform akin to Yelp). Importantly, we leverage user self-reported spending habits documented within Dianping as ground truth for consumption level, creating a robust dataset for supervised learning. By utilizing social login as a bridge—allowing us to link user profiles across these platforms—we have constructed a comprehensive dataset comprising 8,844 users, enabling us to investigate the predictive power of various social media features. Our methodology goes beyond simple feature engineering, exploring both raw textual content and latent representations derived from the social media data. We extract topic distributions using topic modeling techniques, enabling us to understand the themes and subjects that resonate with different consumption groups. Further, we analyze user following behavior to identify influencer clusters and assess their correlation with spending patterns. The core contribution of this work lies in demonstrating that online social media content demonstrably possesses predictive power for offline restaurant consumption level. Moreover, through qualitative feature analysis, we delve into the nuances of word usage, topic interests, and following patterns that distinguish higher and lower consumption groups, offering a deeper understanding of how online expression reflects offline behavior. The ability for machines to understand the relationships between concepts and their associated properties – the attributes that define them – is a cornerstone of true semantic understanding. While lexical resources like WordNet have made significant strides in codifying conceptual knowledge, they often remain limited in their expressiveness, particularly concerning the richness of descriptive attributes that human understanding readily encompasses. For instance, WordNet might define "bird" as a hypernym of "animal," but it lacks a systematic way to capture common attributes like "has feathers," "can fly," or "lays eggs" in a structured, computationally accessible manner. This limitation hinders downstream applications like question answering, commonsense reasoning, and knowledge graph completion, which heavily rely on robust representations of conceptual attributes. Existing methods for enriching lexical resources with attributes frequently rely on ad-hoc heuristics, such as co-occurrence statistics, pattern matching, or manual curation. While these approaches can yield some valuable information, they often suffer from several critical drawbacks. Heuristics are susceptible to biases in the training data, struggle to generalize to unseen concepts, and lack a principled framework for disambiguating multiple plausible attributes. Manual curation, while capable of producing high-quality annotations, is a prohibitively expensive and time-consuming endeavor, severely limiting its scalability. Furthermore, these methods typically lack a probabilistic framework, making it difficult to quantify the uncertainty associated with attribute assignments and to rank potential attributes in terms of their relevance to a given concept. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel approach grounded in Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), a powerful probabilistic model frequently employed in topic modeling and natural language processing. Our work leverages the latent structure inherent in LDA to automatically infer both new concepts and their associated attributes from large text corpora. The core intuition is that a concept's attributes are likely to co-occur with text passages describing the concept, and these co-occurrences can be modeled as latent "topics" representing meaningful properties. By applying LDA to a corpus of text passages annotated with concepts, we can discover latent topics that correspond to plausible attributes for those concepts. This allows us to move beyond simple co-occurrence counts and capture more nuanced semantic relationships. This paper introduces a set of Bayesian methods for extending WordNet with new concepts and, critically, for annotating existing concepts with generic property fields – or attributes – derived from text data. We envision our approach as a mechanism for automatically expanding the descriptive power of WordNet, bridging the gap between its hierarchical structure and the rich constellation of attributes that characterize concepts in human understanding. Our contributions lie in formulating a principled, probabilistic framework using LDA, rigorously evaluating its performance on two key dimensions – the precision of ranked attribute lists and the overall quality of attribute assignments to WordNet concepts – and demonstrating significant improvements over existing heuristic-based methods. We argue that our LDA-based approach drives considerably improved specificity of attribute assignments for each concept, enabling more accurate and robust semantic reasoning in downstream applications. In the following sections, we detail our methodology, present experimental results with established benchmarks, and discuss potential avenues for future research.

The challenge of machine translation (MT) into morphologically rich languages has consistently spurred research exploring techniques to mitigate data sparsity and improve translation quality. One prevalent approach involves segmenting the target language vocabulary into subword units – morphemes or smaller segments – during training. This segmentation effectively increases the number of training examples, particularly for less frequent words, by representing them as combinations of more common subword units. For instance, in Arabic, a highly agglutinative language, a single word can convey a significant amount of grammatical information through prefixes, suffixes, and infixes. Segmenting such words into their constituent morphemes allows the MT system to learn statistical associations between these smaller units, thereby reducing the impact of rare, full-word occurrences. However, this segmentation strategy introduces a non-trivial complication: the need for a desegmentation step. After the MT system generates a sequence of subword units during decoding, these segments must be recombined into plausible, valid words in the target language. Traditionally, this desegmentation process has often been handled as a post-processing stage, separate from the core decoding process. This separation is suboptimal because it prevents the decoder from directly considering the impact of desegmentation on overall translation fluency and adequacy. The 1-best desegmentation approach, where a single, predefined rule or heuristic is applied to combine segments, is commonly employed, but this neglects the richness of potential valid word formations and can lead to unidiomatic or even incorrect target language output. This paper addresses this limitation by proposing a novel approach: decoder-integrated morphological desegmentation. Our method aims to seamlessly integrate the desegmentation process within the phrase-based decoder, enabling the system to dynamically consider the resulting words during the search for the optimal translation. Crucially, our framework facilitates the incorporation of word-level language models (WLMs) directly into the decoding process. Existing phrase-based models typically operate on subword units, precluding the use of WLMs, which are known to capture higher-order word dependencies and improve fluency. By allowing the decoder to evaluate the quality of entire words, formed from the segmented output, we enable a more informed search for the best translation. Our core innovation lies in reformulating the decoding problem to account for the potential desegmentation outcomes at each step. We introduce features that explicitly model the likelihood of different word formations given the current decoder state, enabling the phrase-based decoder to favor translations that result in fluent and grammatically correct target language words. This represents a significant departure from existing approaches, which treat desegmentation as an afterthought. We hypothesize that this tight integration of segmentation and desegmentation will lead to substantial improvements in translation quality, particularly for morphologically complex languages. To validate this hypothesis, we present extensive experiments on a large-scale English-to-Arabic translation task, demonstrating that our method significantly outperforms a strong 1-best desegmentation baseline. Our results underscore the importance of considering desegmentation as an integral part of the MT decoding process and highlight the potential of decoder-integrated approaches for improving the translation of morphologically rich languages.

Automated essay scoring (AES) has emerged as a critical technology in education, offering the potential for scalable feedback and assessment in writing instruction. Traditional AES systems, while demonstrating utility, have historically been constrained by a reliance on meticulously crafted, hand-engineered features. These features encompass a wide spectrum of linguistic characteristics, ranging from syntactic complexity metrics like average sentence length and number of clauses, to lexical diversity measures such as Type-Token Ratio, and even stylistic aspects like the frequency of passive voice constructions. While significant progress has been made in feature engineering for AES, the process remains a challenging and time-consuming endeavor. The performance of these systems is intrinsically linked to the potency and relevance of the features selected; a poorly designed feature set can severely limit scoring accuracy and fairness. Furthermore, the expertise required to identify and implement effective features necessitates specialized knowledge, posing a barrier to widespread adoption and customization. The core problem, then, lies in the bottleneck of manual feature engineering. Existing approaches necessitate a deep understanding of both linguistics and the specific scoring criteria of the essay prompts being evaluated. This leads to systems that are often prompt-dependent, requiring substantial re-engineering whenever the assessment task changes. Moreover, the subjective nature of effective feature selection can introduce bias and limit the generalizability of the AES models. Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly in natural language processing, offer an intriguing alternative to this feature-centric paradigm. Neural networks possess the remarkable ability to automatically learn hierarchical representations from raw data, circumventing the need for explicit feature definition. This capacity is particularly appealing in the context of AES, where the subtle nuances of writing quality are difficult to capture through a finite set of engineered features. This paper explores the application of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, to the task of AES. Our approach aims to directly model the relationship between an essay and its corresponding score, without any manual feature engineering. We hypothesize that LSTMs, with their ability to capture long-range dependencies in sequential data, are well-suited to understand the complex linguistic patterns indicative of strong writing. We investigate various architectural configurations and training strategies to optimize for AES performance. Our research contributes to the field by demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of a purely neural approach to AES, offering a pathway towards more robust, adaptable and potentially fairer essay scoring systems. We present a comprehensive evaluation of our models against a strong baseline system employing traditional feature engineering techniques, showcasing significant improvements in scoring accuracy while eliminating the laborious feature engineering step. Through careful analysis of model behavior, we also aim to garner insights into the linguistic features that the neural networks implicitly learn during the scoring process.

The ability to understand and reason about time is fundamental to human comprehension, yet remains a significant challenge for natural language processing systems. Question answering (QA) tasks, in particular, often require detailed temporal reasoning to produce accurate and informative responses. While advancements in deep learning have demonstrated remarkable progress in various NLP areas, specifically extracting temporal information – understanding *when* events occurred and their relationships – remains an open research problem. Current QA systems frequently struggle to effectively incorporate temporal knowledge, especially when it necessitates navigating complex sentence structures and drawing inferences across multiple sentences or even entire documents. Temporal Information Extraction (TIE) aims to identify and classify temporal relations between events described in text. These relations encompass a broad spectrum, including temporal order (e.g., before, after), duration, frequency, and creation times. Existing approaches to TIE often rely on complex feature engineering, hand-crafted rules, or sophisticated model architectures tailored to specific temporal relations. This specialization leads to a fragmented landscape with models often performing well in narrow domains but lacking generalizability to diverse textual contexts. Moreover, many such systems struggle with the inherent ambiguity in natural language, leading to classification errors and hindering reliable temporal reasoning for QA. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a novel, unified framework for TIE that leverages syntactic dependencies within an LSTM-based architecture. Transliteration mining, the task of automatically identifying mappings between characters or character sequences across different writing systems, has emerged as a crucial component in a range of natural language processing (NLP) applications. Existing NLP models often struggle with languages employing different scripts, particularly when dealing with low-resource languages or those with complex phonetic correspondences. Manual creation of transliteration lexicons is incredibly time-consuming and often impractical, highlighting the need for robust and automated approaches. Current transliteration mining techniques typically rely on statistical methods, alignment algorithms, and dictionary-based approaches. While these methods can be effective in simpler cases, they frequently falter when faced with nuances in orthography, contextual variations in transliteration patterns, and the inherent ambiguity present when mapping characters between unrelated scripts. Furthermore, many existing methods treat transliteration as a purely sequential problem, overlooking the structural relationships and dependencies that exist between characters and character sequences within comparable or parallel text. These limitations inspire the need for more sophisticated models that can leverage contextual information and reason about possible transliteration mappings in a more holistic and informed manner. In this paper, we address these challenges by presenting an enhanced transliteration mining technique based on a generative graph reinforcement model. Our core innovation lies in representing potential transliteration mappings as a bipartite graph, where nodes represent characters or character sequences in the source and target languages, and edges represent potential transliterations. This graph structure allows us to explicitly model the relationships and dependencies between corresponding elements across languages, providing a richer representation compared to purely sequential approaches. We then employ a graph reinforcement algorithm to iteratively refine and enrich this initial mapping network. Critically, we incorporate a link reweighting mechanism that dynamically adjusts the strength of connections based on their likelihood of representing valid transliterations. This mechanism allows the model to learn from both positive and negative examples, effectively promoting accurate mappings while suppressing erroneous ones. Our approach distinguishes itself through its ability to learn and infer complex transliteration patterns beyond what can be extracted through simple alignment techniques. By leveraging graph-based reasoning and a reinforcement learning framework, we are able to capture subtle relationships and contextual dependencies that are often missed by traditional methods. We evaluated our enhanced technique on parallel Wikipedia titles across four diverse language pairs – English-Arabic, English-Russian, English-Hindi, and English-Tamil – presenting a comprehensive analysis of its performance against established baselines and state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that our model achieves significant improvements in F1-measure across all language pairs, outperforming the best published results while also exhibiting a greater degree of robustness to noise and variations in transliteration style. This paper details our methodology, presents the experimental results, and discusses the implications of this work for advancing transliteration mining and its contribution to a wider range of cross-lingual NLP applications.

The demand for high-quality, labeled data is a persistent bottleneck in the development and deployment of modern machine learning models, particularly in the realm of natural language processing. Supervised classification, a foundational task driving numerous NLP applications – from sentiment analysis and text summarization to machine translation and information extraction – inherently relies on datasets brimming with accurate, human-annotated examples. However, the creation of such datasets is often a laborious, time-consuming, and consequently, an expensive endeavor. This necessitates a return to supervised learning paradigms, but with a focus on strategies to substantially reduce the annotation burden. Two distinct yet complementary strategies have emerged as promising solutions: active learning and crowdsourcing. Active learning (AL) offers a principled approach to intelligently selecting the most informative instances from a pool of unlabeled data for annotation. Instead of randomly sampling data points for labeling, AL algorithms strategically query the annotator, focusing on examples whose labeling would yield the greatest improvement in model performance. This targeted annotation strategy aims to maximize the information gain per annotation, allowing models to achieve comparable performance with significantly fewer labeled examples. Crowdsourcing, on the other hand, leverages the collective intelligence of a distributed workforce, often via online platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), to obtain annotations at scale. AMT, in particular, provides a readily accessible and cost-effective means to tap into a diverse pool of human annotators. However, crowdsourced annotations are inherently susceptible to noise and variability, stemming from factors such as varying annotator skill levels, interpretation differences, and potential intentional errors. While techniques exist to mitigate this noise, maintaining consistent annotation quality remains a key challenge. Despite the individual success of both active learning and crowdsourcing, their synergistic combination remains relatively unexplored within the NLP community. While both strategies address aspects of the data acquisition problem, they have largely been treated as separate lines of investigation. Integrating them presents a unique opportunity: can AL’s strategic selection of informative instances be effectively harnessed *within* a noisy crowdsourcing environment to achieve even greater efficiency and accuracy? If so, this could revolutionize how we approach data labeling for NLP tasks. This paper investigates this critical question, presenting a comprehensive empirical evaluation of active learning techniques applied within the context of crowdsourced annotation. We examine two common NLP tasks — named entity recognition (NER) and sentiment detection — and demonstrate that active learning significantly outperforms random sampling when applied to noisy annotations obtained via Amazon Mechanical Turk. Our findings underscore the potential of this combined approach to unlock more economical and effective data labeling pipelines, paving the way for more accessible and scalable NLP applications.

The burgeoning field of distributional semantics has revolutionized our ability to model word meaning, offering computational representations that capture semantic relationships based on patterns of co-occurrence in vast text corpora. Models like Word2Vec, GloVe, and more recently, Transformer-based embeddings, have demonstrated remarkable success in a variety of natural language processing tasks, often achieving human-level performance. While these models undeniably capture statistical regularities within language, they are built upon assumptions regarding linguistic usage that may not perfectly align with how humans organize and process semantic information in their mental lexicon. This disconnect presents a critical challenge for leveraging distributional models to advance our understanding of cognitive science, particularly the intricacies of how we perceive and reason about the relationships between words. This paper investigates this crucial intersection of computational linguistics and cognitive psychology, proposing that models derived not from external text resources, but from internal language structures – specifically, comprehensive data on word associations – can provide a more reliable bridge to human judgments of semantic similarity and relatedness. The rationale stems from the intuition that word associations, the spontaneous links that arise in our minds when encountering a particular word, represent a more direct reflection of our internal mental representations compared to the indirect signal gleaned from observing word co-occurrences across millions of documents. Such associations are inherently tied to how we think about words in relation to each other, capturing implicit connections and conceptual relationships not always explicitly evident in documented text. The central argument of this work is that the ‘external’ knowledge captured in text-based distributional models, while undoubtedly valuable, can be supplemented, and even surpassed, by ‘internal’ language models derived from structured data reflecting the associative network of the human mind. We are particularly interested in testing whether the architectural assumptions underpinning current state-of-the-art text-based embedding models – often designed to mimic observed statistical patterns – are truly necessary for achieving high performance in tasks that closely mimic human semantic judgments. We contrast these dominant external models with a novel set of internal language models built upon a new and extensive dataset of word associations, systematically evaluating their performance against established benchmarks of human similarity and relatedness judgments. Our findings demonstrate that these association-based models consistently and significantly outperform contemporary text-based approaches, suggesting that the fundamental source of distributional knowledge – whether derived from external text or internal associative networks – plays a pivotal role in accurately predicting human semantic perception. Beyond simply achieving improved predictive accuracy, this research aims to shed light on the cognitive mechanisms underlying semantic representation, prompting a re-evaluation of the assumptions guiding the design and interpretation of current distributional models and offering new avenues for future research into the psychological basis of language. We explore these questions through a series of experiments, comparing both model architectures and illustrating the potential for integrating psychological insights into the design of more cognitively grounded distributional semantic models. . --- Let me know if you'd like any modifications or additional content added!

While kernel methods offer exceptional predictive performance, their "black box" nature can impede scientific discovery and practical deployment in scenarios demanding interpretability or scalability. This approach allows us to uncover patterns and relationships that might be missed by traditional feature engineering methods. Sentiment analysis has emerged as a crucial area within natural language processing, driving applications ranging from market research to brand monitoring. While traditional sentiment analysis focuses on determining the overall sentiment expressed within a piece of text (e.g., positive, negative, or neutral), a growing body of research acknowledges the limitations of this broad approach.
