By experimenting with these different integration points, we seek to determine the most effective ways to infuse visual context into the translation process. Furthermore, we recognize that training multi-modal NMT models often faces data scarcity. To mitigate this, we investigate the potential of synthetic multi-modal data augmentation. We generate additional training examples by combining existing text-image pairs with variations in language and image content, exploring how this expanded dataset impacts the performance of our models. Our experiments, conducted on the benchmark Multi30k dataset, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach across both English and German translations. Notably, our best multi-modal models consistently outperform comparable PBSMT systems across all evaluation metrics, representing a significant advancement for purely neural models on this dataset. This marks, to our knowledge, the first instance where a fully neural approach surpasses a well-tuned PBSMT system in all metrics on the Multi30k benchmark. We believe that incorporating global visual features into attention-based NMT offers a promising avenue for enhancing translation quality in visually grounded scenarios and contributing to more robust and contextually aware machine translation systems.

The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has witnessed remarkable advances propelled by the rise of pre-trained language models (PLMs) and their ability to capture nuanced semantic information. A foundational element within these models is the word embedding layer, which maps discrete words to continuous vector representations. While these embeddings, often learned through unsupervised objectives on massive text corpora, provide a powerful starting point for downstream tasks, a prevailing practice involves either freezing them during task-specific fine-tuning or leveraging them as static inputs to classification models. This approach, though efficient, potentially limits the model’s ability to fully adapt word representations to the intricacies of the specific task. Consequently, valuable information relevant to the target task can be lost, hindering optimal performance. Temporal relation extraction (TRE) is a particularly challenging NLP task requiring the identification and classification of temporal relationships between events described in text. Its applications span numerous domains, including information retrieval, question answering, and, critically, healthcare. Accurate temporal reasoning is pivotal in clinical narrative understanding, where the chronological sequence of medical events directly impacts diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient safety. Narrative containment, a specific type of temporal relation, denotes the encompassing of one event by another; for instance, a drug administration occurring *during* a surgical procedure. Extracting this relation from complex clinical records requires capturing fine-grained semantic details and temporal dependencies—demands that push the boundaries of existing NLP techniques. Existing TRE systems often rely on linguistic features such as dependency parses, part-of-speech tags, and semantic roles to guide relation classification. However, training data for these features, especially in specialized domains like healthcare, can be scarce and resource-intensive to annotate. Furthermore, even with meticulously crafted linguistic features, the performance of TRE models can be limited by the quality and adaptability of the underlying word representations. Leveraging the strengths of pre-trained embeddings while simultaneously optimizing them for the specific task becomes therefore, a critical objective. Motivated by these considerations, this paper introduces a novel approach to neural temporal relation classification: *word-level loss extensions*. We propose augmenting a standard classification model’s task-specific loss with an unsupervised auxiliary loss that specifically targets the word embedding layer. This dual-objective training paradigm encourages the model to learn word representations that are simultaneously attuned to the task at hand (i.e., identifying temporal relations) and possess richer, more general semantic features derived from the unsupervised pre-training objective. Our hypothesis is that by allowing the word embeddings to *continue* to learn during task-specific fine-tuning, we can achieve a more balanced and effective representation, capturing both task-specific nuances and broader linguistic knowledge. We validate this approach on the widely-used THYME dataset, a benchmark for temporal relation extraction from clinical narratives. Critically, we demonstrate its effectiveness employing only a general-domain part-of-speech tagger as the only external linguistic resource, highlighting the inherent adaptability of our method. We believe that this work offers a significant step towards improving temporal relation extraction accuracy, particularly in resource-constrained settings, and provides a practical framework for enhancing the utility of pre-trained word embeddings in downstream NLP tasks.

The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing has witnessed remarkable progress in understanding and generating human language. At the core of this progress lies the ability to accurately represent and compare semantic meaning, a capability increasingly crucial for tasks ranging from question answering and machine translation to dialogue systems and information retrieval. Among these, Sentence Similarity (SS) stands out as a fundamental evaluation of semantic understanding – the task of determining the degree to which two sentences convey the same meaning. While seemingly simple, SS presents unique challenges compared to semantics tasks operating at the document or paragraph level. The primary hurdle stems from the inherent sparsity of lexical data within individual sentences. Unlike lengthy documents that offer ample context and repeated occurrences of words, sentences often contain a limited vocabulary, leaving substantial gaps in the signal needed to robustly capture their full semantic import. To truly achieve superior SS performance, it is, therefore, vital to move beyond superficial word overlap and delve into a more nuanced representation of individual word meanings and their interplay within a sentence. Current approaches to SS, particularly those relying solely on distributed word embeddings, often struggle to fully address this sparsity issue. While embedding models like Word2Vec and GloVe capture semantic relationships between words, they frequently fail to differentiate between words with similar meanings but different contextual appropriateness. Consider the words "cat" and "dog" – their embeddings might be close, yet their selectional preferences—the environments in which they are typically used—differ significantly. A sentence about "petting a cat" would gain little from conflating "cat" and "dog" semantically. Similarly, simply knowing that ‘happy’ is similar to ‘joyful’ doesn't inherently inform how ‘happy’ contributes to the overall meaning of the sentence, "She felt happy despite the rain." Motivated by these limitations, we propose a novel approach that explicitly leverages and integrates rich lexical semantics into a latent variable model designed to improve sentential semantics for SS. Our central hypothesis posits that enhanced modeling of lexical semantics—capturing both corpus-driven selectional preference information and knowledge-based information regarding word similarity—will directly lead to improved performance on the SS task. Specifically, we incorporate two key sources of lexical information: first, we extract selectional preferences from large corpora using distributional hypothesis, quantifying the propensity of words to co-occur with particular syntactic or semantic categories and enriching the embedding space with context-specific meaning. Second, we integrate pre-existing knowledge about word similarity derived from established lexical resources like WordNet, explicitly modeling semantic relationships beyond simple distributional co-occurrence. By combining these sources within a unified latent variable framework, we aim to create a more complete and robust representation of each word's contribution to the overall sentence meaning. This paper details the architecture and training procedure of this model, presents comprehensive experimental results on two standard SS datasets, and demonstrates that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance among unsupervised systems, highlighting the efficacy of leveraging lexical semantics to bolster sentential understanding. We believe this work offers a significant step towards more robust and contextually aware sentential semantics, paving the way for improved performance across a wider range of NLP tasks.

The burgeoning volume of Electronic Health Record (EHR) data presents unprecedented opportunities for advancing healthcare through data-driven insights. However, realizing this potential hinges on our ability to effectively extract meaningful information from the predominantly unstructured text within EHR notes – physician narratives, discharge summaries, radiology reports, and more. A crucial step in this semantic understanding process is the accurate identification and delineation of medical events, encompassing diagnoses, procedures, medications, adverse drug reactions, and other clinically significant happenings. The ability to automatically detect these events and their associated attributes (e.g., date, dosage, severity) promises transformative applications across the healthcare spectrum. These range from improved clinical decision support and personalized treatment planning to enhanced pharmacovigilance, disease surveillance, and public health monitoring. Current methods for medical event detection largely rely on supervised machine learning techniques, with Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) representing the established state-of-the-art within this domain. Traditional CRF-based approaches typically leverage hand-engineered features meticulously crafted to capture local context around potential event boundaries. While often reliable, these models suffer from limitations inherent to fixed-window feature engineering. The dependence on predefined context windows struggles to capture long-range dependencies and nuances crucial for accurate event detection, particularly when events are described across multiple sentences or contain complex nested relationships. Furthermore, feature engineering is a time-consuming, domain-specific process requiring substantial expertise and manual effort, hindering the scalability and adaptability of these systems across diverse EHR datasets and clinical specialties. Driven by recent advancements in deep learning, we explore the application of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), specifically bidirectional RNNs, to address the challenges associated with conventional CRF-based medical event detection. RNNs excel at processing sequential data, retaining contextual information over variable lengths, and learning complex patterns without relying on explicit feature engineering. Bidirectional RNNs further enhance this capability by considering both past and future context, providing a more holistic understanding of the surrounding text. This allows the model to leverage potentially relevant information from both sides of a given term, a significant advantage in situations where event boundaries or attribute information are ambiguous or dispersed. In this paper, we detail our investigation into the efficacy of bidirectional RNNs for medical event detection within EHR notes. We present a novel framework that utilizes bidirectional RNNs for sequence labeling, directly predicting event labels and attribute tags from the raw text. We compare the performance of our model against established CRF baselines on a benchmark dataset of de-identified EHR notes, demonstrating significant improvements in both precision and recall. Our results showcase the potential of deep learning architectures to overcome the limitations of traditional feature-based approaches, offering a more robust and adaptable solution for unlocking the valuable information contained within EHRs and ultimately leading to better patient care and improved healthcare outcomes. We further explore the impact of different architectural choices and training strategies within the RNN framework, contributing to a deeper understanding of the characteristics that drive performance in this challenging task. Finally, we discuss the limitations of our approach and outline future research directions including exploration with attention mechanisms, incorporation of external knowledge bases, and adaptation to zero-resource or low-resource settings.

Entity linking (EL), the task of disambiguating mentions of entities in text to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB), remains a critical challenge in natural language processing. It acts as a foundational step for numerous downstream applications, including question answering, information retrieval, and knowledge graph completion. While significant progress has been made, existing approaches often struggle to achieve robust performance across diverse domains and with entities exhibiting subtle variations in meaning. Traditional EL systems often rely on intricate feature engineering, leveraging lexical overlap, string similarity, and hand-crafted rules tailored to specific datasets or domains. These systems exhibit limited generalizability and require substantial manual effort for adaptation. Furthermore, many neglect the rich contextual information surrounding entity mentions, failing to fully exploit the nuances of language that can aid in disambiguation. The inherent complexity of EL stems from the need to integrate multiple facets of information. Beyond the superficial textual mention, a comprehensive understanding necessitates consideration of the entity’s descriptive attributes within the KB – its formal definition, properties, and relationships to other entities. Equally important is the contextual evidence—the surrounding text that provides clues about the intended meaning of a mention. Finally, structured knowledge pertaining to the entity’s type hierarchy can offer crucial constraints, guiding the linking process and resolving ambiguities. However, effectively merging these distinct sources of information has proven difficult, with many approaches treating them as separate components or employing shallow integration strategies. In this paper, we introduce a novel neural entity linking system that overcomes these limitations by adopting a joint encoding approach. Our central innovation lies in learning unified, dense representations for entities that seamlessly incorporate information from their KB descriptions, surrounding contexts, and fine-grained type hierarchies. We move away from the reliance on hand-crafted features and domain-specific training by leveraging powerful neural networks to automatically extract and fuse these diverse signals. Our modular architecture allows for flexible incorporation of various data sources, while the shared embedding space ensures that representations are aligned and comparable. The system is explicitly designed for generalizability: it requires no domain-specific training data or manual feature engineering, enabling consistent performance across a wide range of text corpora. Moreover, we address the challenge of linking mentions of “new” entities – those not yet present in the KB. Traditional EL systems often falter in these scenarios. Our approach incorporates a mechanism to effectively "embed" novel entities, allowing the system to accurately link their mentions even without existing KB entries. This ability significantly enhances the robustness and practicality of our system in real-world applications where encountering previously unseen entities is commonplace. Through extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our model performs competitively with, and occasionally surpasses, state-of-the-art EL systems while exhibiting superior generalizability and handling of novel entities. The results highlight the effectiveness of jointly encoding disparate knowledge sources to achieve robust and adaptable entity linking. Volume, Type, Context - these are key. We argue that such a unified representation is key to generalization and facilitating knowledge discovery. We also emphasize the absence of domain-specific training data, which is a vital feature for real-world deployment.

The rapid advancement of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has yielded impressive results, demonstrating near human-level performance on certain language pairs and domains. However, a crucial limitation persists: most NMT systems operate on a sentence-by-sentence basis, overlooking the rich contextual information inherent within longer documents. This myopic view can lead to inconsistencies, repetitions, and a general lack of coherence in the translated text, particularly when dealing with narratives, technical documentation, or any text exhibiting cross-sentence dependencies. The ability to effectively leverage document-level context is therefore paramount to achieving truly fluent and natural-sounding translations. While research exploring context-aware NMT has steadily grown, challenges remain in capturing and integrating this information effectively. Early attempts often relied on simplistic techniques like concatenating surrounding sentences or employing static context vectors. These approaches, however, struggle to represent the dynamic and nuanced nature of discourse, failing to adequately model the shifting focus and evolving relationships between sentences within a document. More sophisticated methods have explored the incorporation of memory networks or external knowledge sources, often introducing significant computational complexity and requiring substantial labeled data. Motivated by these challenges, we propose a novel Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) specifically designed for document-level neural machine translation. Our approach builds upon the established strengths of attention-based NMT models, but introduces a crucial layer of hierarchical abstraction. Instead of treating the document as a flat sequence of sentences, our model explicitly structures it, first encoding each sentence individually and then aggregating these sentence-level representations into a document-level context vector. Critically, the document-level context is not injected as a static feature, but rather dynamically conditioned on the NMT model's *own* hidden states during decoding. This allows the decoder to selectively attend to relevant document context at each translation step, leading to more contextually appropriate and coherent outputs. The HAN architecture integrates seamlessly with existing NMT frameworks, offering a relatively straightforward modification. We hypothesize that the hierarchical structure allows our model to capture both local sentence-level nuances and global document-level themes, contributing to a more holistic understanding of the source text. Furthermore, we anticipate that the encoder and decoder will benefit from context in distinct, yet complementary ways; the encoder refining sentence representations with broader document awareness, while the decoder utilizes this information to guide translation decisions. This contrasts with some prior approaches where context is treated as a uniform influence across the entire translation process. In this work, we demonstrate empirically that our hierarchical attention mechanism indeed leads to significant improvements in translation quality, surpassing state-of-the-art context-aware NMT methods and achieving substantial gains over strong NMT baselines across several benchmark datasets. We believe that the HAN represents a significant step forward in enabling document-level NMT, paving the way for more fluent, coherent, and human-like machine translation. Our paper proceeds as follows: (1) we present the details of our Hierarchical Attention Network architecture; (2) we describe our experimental setup including datasets and evaluation metrics; (3) we analyze the experimental results and discuss the implications of our findings; and (4) we conclude with a summary of our contributions and outline avenues for future research.

The burgeoning field of opinion mining has traditionally focused on sentiment analysis – determining the polarity (positive, negative, or neutral) of text towards entities. However, a crucial yet comparatively less explored area is *opinion inference*, particularly when dealing with opinions expressed about events that have discernible effects on those entities. Consider the statement, "The new policy sparked widespread protests." Here, the policy (the entity) is indirectly evaluated through the lens of the protests (the event). These events, which we term “+/-effect events,” inherently carry a valence – either positive or negative – depending on the consequences they entail for the entity in question. Recognizing and understanding these relationships is critical for a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of expressed opinions. For example, a company might receive positive sentiment regarding a new product launch (the event) because it ultimately leads to increased sales and stock value (positive effect on the entity). Conversely, a recall announcement (an event) can trigger negative sentiment toward the company due to financial losses and reputational damage (negative effect). Current opinion inference approaches often struggle when dealing with these +/-effect events. Many existing sentiment lexicons operate at the word level, failing to account for the contextual nuances and sense disambiguation required to accurately determine the opinion expressed about an event’s impact. The word “impact,” for instance, can have drastically different connotations depending on whether it refers to a positive or negative influence. Without sense-level granularity, these lexicons risk misinterpreting the sentiment associated with the event and consequently, the opinion regarding the entity. This paper addresses the challenge of creating a sense-level lexicon, which we call +/-EffectWordNet, specifically designed to support opinion inference in the context of +/-effect events. Our core hypothesis is that by representing event senses rather than just individual words, we can significantly improve the accuracy and granularity of opinion inference models. To achieve this, we propose a hybrid approach that leverages the rich structural information of WordNet with the descriptive power of gloss definitions. We employ a graph-based method to exploit WordNet’s relational structure, capturing semantic connections between event-related terms. Simultaneously, we utilize a standard classifier trained on glosses – the textual definitions of WordNet senses – to further refine the sense classifications. The synergy between these two methods, integrated in a hybrid architecture, proves particularly efficacious and yields the best results. Beyond simply constructing a lexicon, we also investigate its utility in guiding manual annotation efforts. A key limitation in lexicon creation is the potential for overlooking subtle or previously uncharacterized senses. We demonstrate that our model effectively identifies potentially overlooked +/-effect senses, acting as a valuable tool to expand the lexicon beyond its initial seed set. This ability to guide annotation is pivotal for improving the lexicon’s completeness and robustness, ultimately leading to more accurate and contextually aware opinion inference systems. In essence, this work contributes a novel lexicon specifically tailored for +/-effect opinions and provides a methodology to efficiently expand and refine it, paving the way for more sophisticated opinion analysis systems.

The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) is increasingly focused on enabling machines to understand and manipulate text in ways that mirror human cognitive processes. Among these processes, simplification stands out as a crucial element in making information accessible, adaptable, and ultimately, more useful across diverse contexts. Sentence compression, a specific form of text simplification, aims to reduce the length of a sentence while preserving its core meaning. Traditionally, sentence compression research has primarily focused on monolingual scenarios, tackling the challenge within a single language. However, the globalized nature of information and the rise of multilingual NLP applications necessitate a shift towards cross-lingual approaches. This paper addresses this critical need by exploring the challenges and opportunities inherent in *parallel sentence compression* – the task of generating compressed versions of sentences that are aligned across two or more languages. The motivation behind parallel sentence compression stems from a growing recognition of its potential to enhance a wide spectrum of multilingual NLP tasks. Consider, for example, machine translation (MT). By compressing the source sentences *before* translation, we may improve the quality and efficiency of the MT system, particularly for languages with significant syntactic differences or complex sentence structures. Similarly, parallel sentence compression can benefit cross-lingual information retrieval, enabling more effective matching of queries and documents across languages by focusing on the core semantic content. Furthermore, it can be utilized in cross-lingual summarization to produce concise and coherent summaries that are aligned across languages. The benefits extend to other applications as well, including parallel meaning representation and cross-lingual paraphrase generation. Ultimately, the ability to generate parallel compressions opens avenues for creating more robust and effective multilingual NLP systems. However, parallel sentence compression introduces unique complexities compared to its monolingual counterpart. The primary challenge lies in ensuring that the compression process preserves not just the meaning of individual sentences, but also the *parallelism* between them. A naive compression approach, applied independently to each language, risks disrupting the alignment and negating the advantages of having parallel data. Considerations such as lexical overlap, syntactic structure, and semantic equivalence become far more intricate when dealing with two (or more) distinct languages. We need methods that explicitly account for these inter-lingual relationships while simultaneously optimizing for compression rate and meaning preservation. In this work, we investigate two contrasting approaches for performing parallel sentence compression. The first leverages shared semantic representations between languages to guide the compression process, ensuring that the core meaning is maintained across both languages. The second explores the exploitation of parallel syntactic structures to identify candidate compression points that are likely to be consistent across languages. We evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches on a parallel corpus of news articles, comparing their performance in terms of compression rate, meaning preservation (measured through human evaluation), and alignment maintenance. We aim to provide valuable insights into the design and implementation of effective parallel sentence compression systems, paving the way for more sophisticated and versatile multilingual NLP tools. The following sections detail our methodology, experimental setup, results, and a comprehensive discussion of the implications of our findings.

The task of syntactic analysis – encompassing word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and dependency parsing – forms a cornerstone of natural language understanding, crucial for downstream applications ranging from machine translation to information retrieval. Chinese, due to its unique characteristics – primarily the absence of explicit word delimiters and the rich morphological complexity reflected in its characters – presents a particularly challenging landscape for these tasks. Traditional approaches to Chinese syntactic analysis have largely relied on non-neural, feature-engineered models, often employing a pipeline architecture where the output of one sub-task (e.g., word segmentation) serves as input to the next (e.g., POS tagging). While seemingly straightforward, this pipeline approach suffers from a significant limitation: error propagation. Errors made in the initial stages of the pipeline cascade through subsequent stages, ultimately degrading the overall analysis quality. Recent advances in deep learning have revolutionized many areas of NLP, yet their application to joint Chinese syntactic analysis has lagged behind. Prior attempts have primarily focused on integrating neural networks into pipeline architectures, effectively continuing the problem of error propagation while introducing the computational overhead of neural models. True joint models, which process the entire input sequence simultaneously and allow for information sharing between the tasks, are rare in the Chinese NLP community and typically still rely on hand-crafted features. The modularity of these approaches restricts the model's capability to capture intricate inter-dependencies among different linguistic levels. This paper introduces a novel neural joint model for Chinese word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing, representing a significant step towards addressing the challenges of joint Chinese syntactic analysis. Our work is, to the best of our knowledge, the first neural approach to fully joint Chinese analysis, purposefully designed to mitigate the error propagation issue inherent in pipeline models. We move beyond simply integrating neural components into a pipeline and present a unified, end-to-end model that learns to perform all three tasks concurrently. A critical innovation within our model is the incorporation of character-string embeddings alongside traditional word embeddings. Previous research has demonstrated the importance of word embeddings in dependency parsing; however, directly applying them in a truly joint setting proves problematic due to the complexities of word segmentation itself. By learning embeddings from Chinese character sequences, we enable the model to better handle ambiguous word boundaries and effectively represent morphological information, contributing to improved performance across all three tasks. Furthermore, we investigate the effectiveness of bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (bi-LSTM) networks, a powerful recurrent neural network architecture, within our joint model, experimenting with reduced feature engineering to demonstrate its efficiency and scalability. Our experimental results, evaluated on benchmark Chinese datasets, demonstrate that our proposed joint model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems in word segmentation and POS tagging, and achieves comparable or superior accuracy in dependency parsing. We believe this work paves the way for more robust and accurate Chinese syntactic analysis systems, bringing us closer to a more comprehensive understanding of the language. The ability to train a single model for multiple related tasks, while avoiding error propagation and leveraging the power of neural networks, offers a compelling path forward for Chinese NLP research.

Ontologies serve as critical knowledge repositories, meticulously structuring types and relationships within specific domains. Their semantic clarity underpins a wide range of applications, from intelligent search and data integration to automated reasoning and knowledge discovery. A pervasive challenge in knowledge engineering, however, arises when multiple ontologies are developed independently to address the same domain. These “parallel” ontologies, while potentially covering overlapping concepts, exist in isolation, hindering a holistic understanding and limiting the potential for knowledge reuse and extension. The task of establishing correspondences, or ‘alignments,’ between entities across these ontologies—linking equivalent or related concepts—is therefore of paramount importance. Ontology matching, the automated process of identifying these alignments, presents a significant obstacle due to the inherent complexities of semantic representation and the often-subtle differences in terminology and structure across ontologies. Traditional ontology matching approaches have relied heavily on hand-crafted features, linguistic patterns, and similarity measures derived from lexical overlap or structural properties. While effective in some cases, these methods often struggle to generalize across diverse ontologies and are highly sensitive to the quality and availability of domain-specific knowledge. More recently, representation learning techniques, particularly those leveraging word embeddings, have shown promise in capturing semantic relationships and enabling more robust alignment. However, existing approaches often require labeled data, hindering their applicability when source ontologies are not accompanied by pre-existing alignment correspondences—a common scenario in practice. In this paper, we introduce DeepAlignment, a novel and fully unsupervised methodology for ontology entity matching. DeepAlignment leverages the power of pre-trained word vectors but goes beyond simply using them as direct entity representations. Our core innovation lies in a targeted refinement process that adapts these general-purpose word vectors to the specific needs of ontology matching. We employ a technique that subtly adjusts the vector space, effectively generating entity descriptions that emphasize features relevant to semantic similarity within an ontological context, without relying on any manually curated alignment data. This refinement is achieved through a carefully designed objective function that promotes alignment coherence while preserving the inherent semantic richness of the original word embeddings. The absence of explicit supervision during the refinement phase is a key differentiator, allowing DeepAlignment to be effectively applied to a broad range of parallel ontologies, regardless of the availability of training data. We hypothesize that this tailored representation learning approach effectively bridges the gap between general semantic understanding, captured by pre-trained word vectors, and the specific requirements of assessing equivalence and relatedness between ontological entities. The refined word vectors enable a more nuanced comparison, capturing subtle semantic nuances often missed by traditional methods. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive empirical evaluations using standard ontology matching benchmarks. Our results demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing state-of-the-art techniques, highlighting the substantial benefits of utilizing representation learning, specifically with this refined word vector approach, for the task of unsupervised ontology matching. These findings suggest that DeepAlignment offers a compelling solution for unifying and extending knowledge across disparate ontological resources. We proceed by first outlining related work in ontology matching and representation learning, then detailing the architecture and training methodology of DeepAlignment. Following a comprehensive description of our experimental setup and evaluation metrics, we present the results and conclude with a discussion of potential future research directions.

The digitization of healthcare records has ushered in an era of unprecedented data availability, offering the potential to revolutionize clinical decision-making, research, and healthcare administration. A crucial component of these electronic health records (EHRs) is the presence of medical codes – standardized alphanumeric identifiers representing diagnoses, procedures, and other aspects of patient care. These codes, predominantly utilizing systems like ICD (International Classification of Diseases) and CPT (Current Procedural Terminology), are vital for billing, reimbursement, quality reporting, and epidemiological studies. However, the process of assigning these codes to patient encounters is fraught with challenges. Currently, this task predominantly relies on human coders, a process that is both labor-intensive and susceptible to inter-coder variability, leading to potential inaccuracies and inefficiencies. The sheer volume of clinical data generated daily necessitates automated solutions to alleviate this bottleneck and improve the reliability of code assignment. While various machine learning approaches have demonstrated promise in automating medical code prediction, a significant limitation remains – the "black box" nature of these models. Many existing methods, particularly deep learning models, excel at predictive accuracy but offer limited insight into *why* a particular code was assigned. This lack of transparency is particularly problematic in the medical domain, where understanding the reasoning behind a clinical decision is paramount. Physicians require not only accurate predictions but also explanations that align with their clinical judgment and allow them to validate the model’s reasoning. Simply presenting a predicted code without justification is insufficient; it undermines trust and limits the potential for incorporating these predictions into clinical workflows. Furthermore, the absence of annotated connections between the clinical text and the assigned codes constitutes a critical gap in current datasets and training paradigms. This hinders the development of models that can learn the nuanced relationships between linguistic patterns in a patient's medical history and the corresponding diagnoses and treatments. Without explicit connections, models struggle to identify the specific textual evidence supporting a code assignment. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel attentional convolutional network architecture designed for explainable prediction of medical codes from clinical text. Our approach leverages the power of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to capture local patterns and dependencies within the textual data, while employing an attention mechanism to highlight the most relevant segments of the clinical note for each specific code. This attention mechanism allows us to generate explanations alongside code predictions, effectively revealing the textual evidence the model deemed most important. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in code prediction, achieving a precision@8 of 0.71 and a Micro-F1 score of 0.54. Critically, we conduct a rigorous interpretability evaluation involving a physician, confirming that the attention weights consistently identify meaningful and clinically relevant phrases justifying the assigned codes. Our work moves beyond solely focusing on predictive accuracy to prioritize explainability, paving the way for more reliable, trustworthy, and clinically useful automated medical coding systems. We believe that this focus on transparency unlocks the full potential of machine learning in healthcare, enabling clinicians to collaborate with these systems and ultimately improve patient care.

The ubiquity of smartphones and the increasing sophistication of voice assistants have fueled a dramatic rise in voice-based interactions, fundamentally altering how users access information and services. A particularly significant and rapidly growing application of this trend lies in local business discovery – users increasingly rely on voice search to find nearby restaurants, shops, and service providers. This paradigm shift presents both incredible opportunity and considerable challenges for speech recognition technology. While advancements in automatic speech recognition (ASR) have been remarkable in broad domains, the specific nuances of local business names—often containing unique spellings, regional variations, and uncommon terminology—pose a significant hurdle to accurate transcription. The current reliance on large, nationwide language models (LMs) often proves inadequate in this context, resulting in frequent recognition errors and frustrating user experiences. The core issue is that a single, monolithic language model, trained on a vast corpus of general text, struggles to capture the localized linguistic patterns prevalent within specific geographic regions. Business names, in particular, are a rich source of these patterns. They may incorporate local landmarks, family names common to the area, or historical terminology that deviates significantly from standard language usage. Consequently, even with high-quality acoustic models, ASR errors become rampant when attempting to recognize these names, hindering the user's ability to quickly and accurately connect with the businesses they seek. This paper addresses this critical gap by introducing a novel approach to language model construction specifically tailored for local business voice search: Geo-Centric Language Models (GCLMs). Our algorithm dynamically generates language models that are geographically relevant, leveraging the density of local businesses to determine the appropriate scope and granularity of the model. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on pre-built national or regional LMs, GCLMs adapt to the user’s precise location, providing a focused and highly accurate language representation of the surrounding business landscape. This granularity is crucial; a model encompassing an entire state might be too broad to effectively capture the specific linguistic features of a single city or neighborhood, while a model built for a tiny area may overlook broader patterns. Furthermore, our methodology is designed for efficiency. We propose a system where these powerful, localized language models can be pre-compiled and stored, enabling rapid and real-time recognition without incurring the computational overhead of on-the-fly model generation. This is particularly important for mobile voice search applications, where latency can significantly impact user engagement. This pre-compilation strategy allows us to balance accuracy and speed, crucial for providing a seamless user experience. Our experimental results, conducted using a real-world dataset of spoken business listing name queries from a business directory assistance service, demonstrate the substantial benefits of our GCLM approach. We achieved a remarkable 16.8% absolute improvement in recognition accuracy compared to a nationwide language model, along with a three-fold speedup in recognition time. These findings underscore the potential of geo-centric language modeling to revolutionize local business voice search and deliver a significantly more effective and user-friendly experience. The paper will detail the algorithm, the dataset, the experimental setup, and a thorough analysis of the results, highlighting the contributions of this work to the field of spoken language understanding.

The sheer scale of modern economic data can be overwhelming. News headlines frequently feature enormous numbers – billions of dollars in corporate acquisitions, trillions in national debts, and countless millions in humanitarian aid disbursements. While these figures convey magnitude, they often lack crucial context, leaving readers struggling to grasp the real-world implications. How much *is* 131 million dollars? While a simple declaration of the amount offers no real understanding, placing it within relatable frameworks—such as comparing it to everyday expenditures or the cost of tangible goods—can significantly improve comprehension. However, manually crafting such contextual comparisons is a laborious and time-consuming process, limiting their widespread use. This paper addresses the challenge of making large numbers more accessible through automated generation of perspective-providing descriptions. We introduce a novel task: automatically generating short, intuitive descriptions – which we term “perspectives” – that contextualize numeric mentions. A perspective for $131 million, for example, might be "about the cost to employ everyone in Texas over a lunch period." This approach leverages the power of narrative and relatable analogies to bridge the gap between abstract quantities and human understanding. Existing approaches to numerical understanding predominantly focus on tasks like numerical reasoning or question answering about numbers. While valuable, they don't inherently address the problem of grounding numbers in relatable contexts. Simple numerical comparisons (e.g., "131 million is more than 100 million") are insufficient to convey a true sense of scale. Generating descriptive perspectives, however, requires more than just numerical fluency; it necessitates connecting numbers to the broader world—to concepts, activities, and other quantities familiar to everyday experience. To facilitate this, we propose a system built on a compositional approach. Our framework decomposes the perspective generation process into two distinct, interconnected stages: formula construction and description generation. Formula construction identifies and composes relevant factual relationships from a knowledge base, creating mathematical expressions that directly relate the target number to other meaningful quantities. Critically, these formulas are ranked based on factors like their familiarity, numerical proximity to the target value, and semantic compatibility. The subsequent description generation stage leverages a sequence-to-sequence recurrent neural network to translate the selected formula into a fluent and natural language description. We believe this compositional approach is vital. By explicitly constructing and evaluating intermediate formulas, our system moves beyond purely statistical or pattern-matching techniques, providing a more interpretable and controllable mechanism for generating perspectives. Furthermore, it allows us to incorporate explicit knowledge about the world, ensuring the generated descriptions are factually grounded and logically sound. The resulting system demonstrably outperforms a non-compositional baseline across both formula construction and description generation, yielding impressive improvements in both F1 score and BLEU score respectively. We discuss our dataset creation, model architecture, and experimental results in detail to showcase the efficacy of our approach in making large numbers more readily comprehensible. Ultimately, this work aims to empower both humans and machines to better process and understand the ever-increasing volume of numerical information that pervades our world.

The burgeoning field of natural language processing has consistently demonstrated the power of distributed word embeddings in capturing semantic relationships and enabling significant advancements in various downstream tasks. From sentiment analysis and machine translation to question answering and information retrieval, dense vector representations of words – such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText – have become a cornerstone of modern NLP pipelines. However, a persistent challenge lies in effectively representing the polysemy inherent in natural language – the fact that a single word can possess multiple, distinct meanings depending on the context. Traditional word embedding models often conflate these disparate senses into a single, averaged representation, leading to a loss of nuanced information and potentially hindering performance on tasks requiring fine-grained semantic understanding. Addressing this limitation, the concept of multi-sense word embeddings has gained considerable traction. These models aim to learn distinct vector representations for each sense of a word, allowing for a more accurate and contextually appropriate portrayal of its meaning. While various approaches to building multi-sense embeddings exist, many rely heavily on either painstakingly curated sense inventories (e.g., WordNet-based methods) or complex, task-specific training procedures. Furthermore, leveraging cross-lingual information to enhance multi-sense embeddings remains an area ripe for exploration, particularly given the potential for richer semantic insights gained through parallel data. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to learning multi-sense word embeddings that uniquely combines monolingual and bilingual information within a unified framework. Our method, termed Bilingual Learning of Multi-sense Embeddings with Discrete Autoencoders (BLME-DAE), departs from traditional approaches by employing a discrete autoencoder architecture to enforce a structured latent space representing word senses. Crucially, our model operates with a probabilistic sense disambiguation component, which dynamically selects the most appropriate sense representation based on both the local monolingual context and information gleaned from a parallel sentence in another language. This dual-contextualization provides a richer signal for sense identification, enabling the model to capture subtle semantic nuances often missed by solely monolingual methods. The model’s architecture comprises an encoder that processes both monolingual and bilingual context and employs this information to predict a discrete sense representation – essentially, choosing which of a finite set of potential senses best aligns with the observed input. A decoder component then leverages this selected sense representation to predict surrounding context words. The two modules are trained jointly, encouraging the encoder to generate sense representations that are useful for the decoder in reconstructing the original context. We hypothesize that by incorporating bilingual information, the model can implicitly learn more robust and generalizable sense representations, capitalizing on cross-lingual semantic correspondences. We demonstrate empirically that even when evaluated solely on monolingual data at test time, the multi-sense embeddings learned with our bilingual approach consistently outperform those learned from monolingual data alone across a range of semantic evaluation tasks. This highlights the potential of cross-lingual knowledge transfer to enhance the quality of multi-sense word embeddings, even in scenarios where explicit cross-lingual alignment is not required.

The observation that humans effortlessly coordinate their language use in conversation – a phenomenon known as linguistic alignment – has captivated researchers across disciplines for decades. From phonological mirroring to lexical choices and syntactic structures, conversational partners exhibit a tendency to converge on one another’s linguistic behaviors, ostensibly fostering rapport, understanding, and smooth interaction. A particularly intriguing, and often cited, line of inquiry within this field relates the degree of linguistic alignment to the social dynamics between interlocutors. Specifically, a prevalent hypothesis suggests that individuals perceived as holding higher social power exert a greater influence on their conversational counterparts, receiving proportionally more linguistic alignment than those in subordinate positions. This notion, rooted in established sociological theories about power dynamics, posits that individuals of higher status are afforded greater attentiveness and conformity from those of lower status, manifesting linguistically as a heightened propensity for the latter to adopt the former’s linguistic patterns. Numerous studies, primarily utilizing observational data from naturally occurring conversations, have appeared to lend support to this "power-alignment" hypothesis. Across a variety of contexts – from doctor-patient interactions to workplace meetings, and even casual everyday conversations – researchers have reported a statistically significant positive relationship between perceived power differentials and the degree of alignment observed. These findings have been interpreted as evidence that power not only shapes conversational flow and topic selection, but also subtly influences the fundamental linguistic architecture of interaction, reflecting an unconscious deference to authority or a strategic effort to gain approval. However, a critical aspect often overlooked in these investigations centers on the potential confounding influence of low-level linguistic features. While social power may indeed play a role in shaping conversation, it's increasingly plausible that the observed alignment phenomena are, at least partially, attributable to readily quantifiable characteristics of utterances themselves. Factors such as utterance length, complexity, the presence of specific function words, and even the rate of speech have been shown to influence alignment independently of social status. It's possible that the apparent power effect is not a direct consequence of power dynamics, but rather emerges from a spurious correlation arising from the fact that, for instance, longer utterances may naturally elicit more subsequent convergence, regardless of who produced them. In this paper, we challenge the prevailing assumption that social power is a primary driver of linguistic alignment. We systematically investigate the relationship between power and alignment across two distinct datasets, employing robust logistic regression models to rigorously control for a range of low-level linguistic features. Our analysis reveals a surprising and counterintuitive pattern: the purported power effect on alignment diminishes substantially, and in some cases reverses, when these readily measurable linguistic characteristics are incorporated into the models. These findings suggest that the observed alignment patterns might be more readily explained by cognitive processes associated with linguistic processing, such as the inherent tendency to mirror patterns observed in preceding utterances, rather than by dynamic social hierarchies. We propose that future research exploring social factors in language use should more explicitly attend to the potential of confounding linguistic variables and consider a broader spectrum of cognitive and interactional factors that shape conversational dynamics. Ultimately, our work argues for a recalibration of current understandings, emphasizing the potentially overstated role of social power in shaping the nuanced phenomenon of linguistic alignment.

The accurate identification and representation of predicate-argument dependencies lies at the heart of numerous natural language understanding tasks, including information extraction, question answering, semantic role labeling, and ultimately, the construction of robust knowledge graphs. While traditional dependency parsing approaches have achieved significant success, they often struggle to adequately capture the complexities introduced by long-range dependencies—specifically, those unbounded dependencies that connect elements across substantial distances within a sentence. These unbounded dependencies, which include non-adjacent modification, indirect object constructions, and certain types of relative clauses, can constitute a surprisingly large proportion of the dependencies present in natural language, contributing significantly to overall semantic ambiguity and hindering accurate interpretation. Consequently, robustly recovering these unbounded dependencies remains a crucial challenge in natural language processing. Current approaches to dependency parsing often rely on learning complex probabilistic models over large annotated corpora, necessitating substantial computational resources and sophisticated feature engineering. Furthermore, these models frequently lack principled linguistic grounding, leading to brittle behavior and limited generalization capabilities, particularly when facing novel syntactic structures. Categorial grammars (CGs) offer a compelling alternative paradigm that emphasizes compositional semantics and, crucially, leverages a small, fixed set of combinatorial operations—functors and arguments—to derive sentence structure directly from meaning. This inherent focus on compositional semantics and the relative simplicity of the grammar rules propose advantages in modularity and interpretability. However, standard CGs can be overly restrictive, struggling to express the nuances of natural language syntax without resorting to ad-hoc extensions. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel approach to unbounded dependency recovery predicated on a Generalized Categorial Grammar (GCG). Our GCG builds upon the strengths of traditional CGs by maintaining their inherent semantic clarity and limited rule set, while borrowing from the framework of Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG) in its utilization of a minimal, constraint-based category inventory. This allows us to effectively constrain the possible syntactic configurations while retaining the elegance and efficiency of CGs. The result is a grammar capable of expressing a wide range of syntactic structures, including those involving unbounded dependencies, with a relatively small and readily learnable set of rules. A key contribution of this work is a novel reannotation system designed to seamlessly translate existing syntactic treebanks, originally annotated according to Government and Binding Theory, into our GCG representation. This allows us to leverage and build upon the vast wealth of existing linguistic resources, such as the Penn Treebank, without requiring entirely new annotation efforts. The reannotation process is carefully designed to preserve as much information as possible from the original annotation while conforming to the constraints and structure of the GCG. Finally, we rigorously evaluate the performance of our GCG-based dependency recovery system on the established CoNLL-X shared task benchmark, demonstrating competitive results relative to existing state-of-the-art approaches, while offering a more linguistically grounded and interpretable alternative. We believe this work represents a significant step forward in developing accurate and robust unbounded dependency recovery systems.

The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing has witnessed a significant shift toward approaches capable of handling the complexities and scale of real-world text. Among these advancements, Open Information Extraction (Open IE) stands out as a particularly ambitious endeavor. Unlike traditional Information Extraction (IE) systems that rely on predefined schemas and relations, Open IE aims to automatically extract structured information from unstructured text without requiring a fixed vocabulary of relations or entities. The promise of Open IE is immense: to unlock the vast potential of raw textual data, facilitating knowledge discovery, question answering, and a myriad of other applications that necessitate a deep understanding of the information contained within. However, despite considerable progress, existing Open IE systems still grapple with fundamental challenges that limit their practical utility. While they successfully pull phrases from text that *look* like assertions, the resulting extractions are often plagued by issues of informativeness and coherence. A significant proportion of extracted relations are trivial, containing redundant information or lacking sufficient context to be genuinely meaningful. Furthermore, the extracted triples frequently exhibit internal inconsistencies or semantic implausibilities, rendering them unreliable for downstream tasks. These shortcomings stem from the inherent difficulty in discerning genuine, valuable assertions from the noise of natural language - including complex syntactic structures, ambiguous phrasing, and the subtle nuances of human communication. Previous approaches, like TEXTRUNNER and WOE, while pioneering in their own right, have struggled to effectively address these core problems, frequently producing a flood of low-quality extractions that necessitate extensive post-processing and filtering. In this paper, we tackle these challenges head-on. We argue that the quality of Open IE extractions can be substantially improved by incorporating simple, yet effective, syntactic and lexical constraints that reflect fundamental principles of language structure and meaning. Our central hypothesis is that by focusing on verb-centric relations and applying targeted filtering, we can significantly reduce the ratio of low-quality extractions while maintaining a high recall of meaningful assertions. To this end, we introduce a novel Open IE system, REVERB, built upon the REVERB framework, which integrates two carefully designed constraints - one focusing on syntactic dependency trees and the other leveraging contextual lexical information. We demonstrate that these seemingly simple additions have a surprisingly dramatic impact on the overall performance of the system. Our experiments, conducted on standard Open IE benchmarks, reveal that REVERB achieves a transformative improvement over existing state-of-the-art Open IE systems like TEXTRUNNER and WOE. Specifically, REVERB more than doubles the area under the precision-recall curve, a crucial metric for evaluating the trade-off between precision and recall in information extraction. Furthermore, a substantial portion (over 30%) of REVERB's extractions attain a precision of 0.8 or higher – a level of accuracy previously unattainable by earlier systems. Beyond demonstrating superior quantitative performance, we also provide a detailed qualitative analysis of REVERB’s errors, highlighting areas for future research and outlining potential avenues for further refinement. Our findings underscore the importance of incorporating linguistic knowledge into Open IE systems, paving the way for more robust, informative, and ultimately more useful extraction of knowledge from unstructured text.

The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) relies heavily on the quality of word representations, commonly known as word embeddings. These embeddings, capturing semantic and syntactic relationships between words, serve as foundational building blocks for a vast array of downstream tasks, including machine translation, text classification, sentiment analysis, and question answering. Traditional methods like Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) have demonstrated remarkable success in generating these embeddings, but they typically operate under a fixed dimensionality constraint. Consequently, applications requiring varying embedding dimensions—a frequent occurrence due to differing computational budgets, model architectures, or task specifics—must either re-train embeddings from scratch or resort to less-than-ideal dimensionality reduction techniques. Retraining is computationally expensive, particularly on large corpora, and dimensionality reduction often compromises the integrity of the learned semantic information. This rigidity poses a significant limitation in practical NLP workflows. The challenge, therefore, lies in developing a word embedding methodology that offers inherent flexibility in dimensionality without sacrificing the quality of representation. This paper introduces Right-truncatable Neural Word Embeddings (RT-NWE), a novel approach to training neural word embeddings that addresses this critical issue. Our method departs from traditional training paradigms by employing an iterative, dimension-by-dimension learning strategy, effectively building the embedding vector sequentially. This incremental construction grants RT-NWE a unique and powerful property: any right-truncated version of a generated embedding vector corresponds precisely to the solution of the equivalent, lower-dimensional embedding trained independently. In simpler terms, if we have a 100-dimensional RT-NWE, the first 50 dimensions represent a fully-trained 50-dimensional embedding, the first 75 represent a fully-trained 75-dimensional embedding, and so on, all the way to the full 100 dimensions. This property provides unparalleled adaptability. A single RT-NWE vector can seamlessly accommodate myriad dimensional requirements, enabling downstream applications to dynamically select the appropriate embedding size based on their specific needs. This is particularly beneficial in scenarios involving resource-constrained environments, multi-task learning, or adaptive model architectures. Imagine deploying a model on a mobile device – a lower dimensional embedding can reduce memory footprint and improve inference speed, while retaining the same semantic information originally captured by a larger embedding. This also facilitates experimentation with different embedding sizes without the overhead of repeated training. Moreover, it allows for a gradual increase in embedding dimensionality as more training data becomes available. The RT-NWE framework is readily applicable to existing neural word embedding architectures like Skip-gram and GloVe, requiring minimal modifications to the core training algorithm. The key innovation resides in the iterative construction process and the inherent right-truncatability that results. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing that RT-NWE achieves comparable, and in some cases superior, performance to traditional methods while offering significantly enhanced flexibility in dimensionality control. The remainder of this paper details the methodology, experimental setup, results, and concludes with a discussion of potential future directions.

The challenge of cross-lingual lexical substitution – replacing words in one language with equivalent words in another while preserving meaning and nuances – is a cornerstone problem in machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and multilingual text generation. While traditional approaches often focus on semantic similarity and distributional overlap, a critical, yet frequently overlooked, dimension of lexical meaning lies in its inherent subjectivity. Words, far from being solely objective representations of concepts, often carry emotional connotations and subjective evaluations that vary significantly across languages and cultures. This paper investigates the compelling relationship between word sense subjectivity and the effectiveness of cross-lingual lexical substitution, proposing that accounting for these subjective characteristics can lead to significant improvements in substitution quality. Current cross-lingual lexical substitution methodologies are predominantly built upon distributional semantics, leveraging parallel corpora or comparable datasets to identify potential word mappings based on similar contextual usage patterns. These methods, while successful in many scenarios, frequently stumble when encountering words with multiple senses, particularly those where one sense is predominantly subjective while another is objective. Consider the English word "sick," for instance. While often used objectively to denote illness, it also carries a subjective connotation meaning "excellent" or "cool," especially within informal contexts. A purely distributional approach, lacking awareness of this sense polarization, might struggle to consistently select appropriate substitutions in the target language, potentially introducing unintended sentiment shifts or even semantic inconsistencies. We hypothesize that integrating word sense subjectivity into the substitution process provides a crucial filter for disambiguation, allowing for more accurate and contextually appropriate target language selections. Our line of reasoning stems from the assumption that effective cross-lingual substitution requires not only preserving the core meaning, but also maintaining the emotive impact and subjective tone present in the original text. If a word in the source language conveys a strong emotional sentiment – a subjective characteristic – the corresponding substitute in the target language should ideally reflect a similar emotional weight, even if the literal meaning is slightly altered. This paper introduces a novel framework for incorporating word sense subjectivity into cross-lingual lexical substitution. We leverage existing subjectivity lexicons and sentiment analysis techniques to quantify the subjective polarity of each word sense in both English and Chinese. Our experimental design focuses on English-Chinese substitution, a particularly interesting pairing due to the linguistic and cultural differences that can significantly amplify subjectivity-related challenges. We demonstrate that explicitly accounting for word sense subjectivity can indeed improve substitution accuracy and fluency, even outperforming approaches that incorporate full-fledged, computationally intensive fine-grained word sense disambiguation (WSD) for words possessing both subjective and objective senses. This finding suggests a potential pathway towards more efficient and accurate cross-lingual lexical substitution systems, bypassing the complexities of WSD while still achieving comparable results through a simpler, subjectivity-focused approach. Notably, our results highlight the importance of considering emotional and evaluative aspects of language when bridging linguistic boundaries, opening avenues for future research exploring the broader role of subjectivity in cross-lingual natural language processing. We will explore these ideas, present our methodology, and report our experimental findings in subsequent sections of this paper.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) systems have historically achieved remarkable progress, demonstrating impressive fluency and accuracy across a diverse range of language pairs and topics. However, a persistent challenge remains: the degradation of performance when deploying these models in domains distinct from those on which they were trained. This phenomenon, known as domain shift, stems from the inherent mismatch in vocabulary, style, and topic distributions between the training data (the source domain) and the deployment environment (the target domain). While fine-tuning existing models on limited in-domain data is a common mitigation strategy, acquiring and curating sufficient, high-quality in-domain parallel corpora can be prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, particularly for low-resource languages or specialized domains like legal, medical, or scientific texts. The conventional wisdom in machine learning suggests that increasing the size of the training dataset invariably leads to improved performance; however, this assumption often proves flawed in the context of domain adaptation. Simply appending massive amounts of general-domain data to an in-domain training set can introduce noise and dilute the signal, potentially hindering, rather than enhancing, translation quality. In this paper, we challenge this assumption and propose a novel and efficient approach to domain adaptation for SMT that focuses on *selective* data integration. Instead of utilizing the entirety of a large, general-domain parallel corpus, we advocate for the extraction of a carefully curated "pseudo in-domain" subcorpus – a representative subset of sentences deemed most relevant to the target domain. Our underlying principle is that intelligent data selection can outperform indiscriminate data augmentation, leveraging the vast resources of readily available general-domain data while mitigating the risks of introducing irrelevant noise. We hypothesize that these pseudo in-domain subcorpora, even when significantly smaller than the original corpus (in our experiments, less than 1% of the original size), can be effectively utilized to train small, focused SMT models exhibiting surprisingly high performance, exceeding that of models trained on the full corpus. We introduce three distinct methodologies for selecting these pseudo in-domain sentences based on cross-entropy similarity measures, offering a spectrum of complexity and computational cost. These methods assess the relevance of a general-domain sentence to the target domain by comparing its distribution to that of a reference corpus, providing a ranking reflecting the degree of similarity. We then explore the potential of combining these domain-adapted models, trained on the pseudo in-domain data, with existing in-domain models during the decoding process. This hybrid approach aims to harness the strengths of both domains – the broad knowledge and fluency of the general-domain model and the domain-specific terminology and style of the in-domain model. Our experiments, conducted on a variety of SMT tasks demonstrating significant domain shift, demonstrate that this approach consistently outperforms both baseline models trained on the full general-domain corpus and models trained on limited in-domain data alone. Moreover, the combined in-domain and pseudo in-domain model consistently achieves state-of-the-art results, illustrating the power of targeted data selection and ensemble decoding strategies. This work provides compelling evidence that in domain adaptation, less can indeed be more, and that intelligent data selection is a crucial ingredient for achieving robust and high-quality machine translation across diverse domains.

Nested mention recognition (NMR) – the task of identifying all mentions of entities within a text, accounting for their hierarchical, nested relationships – has emerged as a crucial component of advanced natural language understanding. Traditional entity recognition systems often struggle with identifying complex entities comprised of multiple sub-mentions, particularly in domains where nested structures are prevalent, such as news articles, scientific reports, and legal documents. The failure to accurately capture these nested relationships can significantly impact downstream applications like relation extraction, coreference resolution, and knowledge graph construction, leading to inaccurate inferences and reduced overall system performance. While existing approaches have tackled this challenge, they often rely on feature engineering, complex parsing techniques, or suffer from limited scalability when dealing with long sentences and intricate nested structures. Previous NMR models frequently employ either rule-based systems or statistical models that require extensive feature engineering, limiting their adaptability to different domains and languages. More recent approaches have explored recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for NMR, but many still lack an inherent mechanism for explicitly modeling the hierarchical nesting structure. Graph-based neural networks have also shown promise, but their computational complexity can become prohibitive for longer sentences with multiple nested mentions. Furthermore, many existing models neglect the importance of character-level information, which can be vital for identifying subtle patterns within mention boundaries, especially when dealing with ambiguous phrasing or abbreviations. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel neural transition-based model for nested mention recognition that offers improved scalability, efficiency, and accuracy. Our approach departs from traditional methods by leveraging the well-established principles of transition-based parsing, adapted to effectively model the nested structure of mentions. Rather than directly predicting mention boundaries, our model constructs a "mention forest," a tree-like representation where each node corresponds to a mention and the edges define the nested relationships between them. This allows for a clear and interpretable representation of the mention hierarchy. Crucially, our system employs a shift-reduce architecture, enabling a bottom-up, incremental construction of the mention forest. The action sequence required to build the forest is inherently bounded – specifically, it’s guaranteed to be no more than three times the length of the input sentence, ensuring computational feasibility even for lengthy documents. To effectively manage the state information during this process, we utilize a Stack-LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) network, which efficiently maintains and updates representations of the evolving mention stack. We also incorporate a character-based embedding component to capture fine-grained letter-level information, complementing the word-level context provided by the Stack-LSTM. By combining these techniques, our model learns to recognize nested mentions in a data-driven and scalable manner, without relying on hand-engineered features or complex parsing algorithms. This paper details the architecture and training procedure of our system, and demonstrates its effectiveness through experimental results on the ACE datasets, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance. We believe that our transition-based approach, coupled with the Stack-LSTM and character-level embeddings, offers a significant step forward in nested mention recognition, paving the way for more robust and nuanced entity understanding in various NLP applications.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has historically relied on carefully engineered features to capture the nuances of language and guide the translation process. These features, often informed by linguistic intuition, domain expertise, and extensive experimentation, represent lexical, syntactic, and semantic aspects of the source and target phrases. While effective, the manual feature engineering approach is labor-intensive, requires deep linguistic knowledge, and can struggle to adapt to new domains or language pairs. The pursuit of more robust and adaptable features has spurred research into automatically learning representations that can enhance translation quality. In recent years, deep learning techniques have demonstrated considerable promise in this area, offering the potential to automatically discover complex and subtle patterns in data that might be missed by manual feature design. This paper explores a novel approach to feature learning for phrase-based SMT, leveraging the power of deep autoencoders (DAEs) in a semi-supervised setting. Rather than manually crafting features, we aim to learn new, more effective representations directly from the data. Traditional unsupervised methods, such as using deep belief networks (DBNs) for feature extraction, have shown some benefit. However, these approaches often fail to fully exploit the available, albeit limited, labeled data and can result in features that lack the richness needed to capture complex translation phenomena. Our work builds upon this foundation by introducing a semi-supervised training strategy designed to improve the quality and stability of the learned features. Specifically, we initialize our DAEs with pre-trained parameters from a DBN, benefiting from the unsupervised learning of initial representations. Critically, we then employ the original phrase features – those traditionally used in SMT systems – as a “teacher” signal during a semi-supervised fine-tuning stage. This allows the DAEs to gradually refine their representations, converging towards features that are both effective in extracting meaningful information and aligned with established translation practices.
